title: V. A Sudden Resolution
paragraphs: Fenya was sitting in the kitchen with her grandmother. The two of them were just about to go to bed. They trusted Nazar Ivanovitch to keep watch, so they hadn’t locked the door. Mitya burst in, pounced on Fenya and grabbed her by the throat.
“Tell me, now! Where is she? Who’s she with now, at Mokroe?” he roared furiously.
Both women screamed.
“Aie! I’ll tell you! Aie! Dmitri Fyodorovitch, darling, I’ll tell you everything this minute, I won’t hide a thing,” Fenya gabbled, frightened to death. “She’s gone to Mokroe, to her officer.”
“What officer?” Mitya roared.
“Her officer! The same one she knew before, the one who threw her over five years ago,” Fenya cackled, as fast as the words would come.

Mitya let go of her throat. He stood facing her, deathly pale and unable to speak, but his eyes showed that he had taken it all in, all of it, from the very first word, and had guessed the whole situation. Poor Fenya was in no state to notice whether he understood or not. She sat on the trunk exactly as she had been when he rushed in, shaking all over and holding her hands out in front of her as if to ward off a blow. She seemed to have frozen in that position. Her eyes were wide with fright and fixed on him without a flicker. To make matters worse, both his hands were smeared with blood. He must have touched his forehead with them as he ran, wiping away the sweat, because there were bloody patches on his forehead and on his right cheek. Fenya was close to hysterics. The old cook had leaped up and was staring at him like a madwoman, nearly out of her mind with terror.

Mitya stood for a moment, then dropped mechanically onto a chair beside Fenya. He sat there without thinking, stunned and numb with terror. And yet it was all as clear as day. That officer: he knew about him, he knew all about him. He had heard it from Grushenka herself, and he had known that a letter from the man had arrived a month ago. So for a whole month this had been going on behind his back, right up to the arrival of this new man, and he had never once thought of him! But how could he, how could he have failed to think of him? Why had he forgotten this officer, simply forgotten him the moment he heard of him? That was the question that rose up before him like some monstrous thing. And he stared at this monstrous thing in horror, going cold with horror.

But suddenly, as gently and mildly as an affectionate child, he began talking to Fenya, as if he had completely forgotten how he had just frightened and hurt her. He started to question her with a thoroughness that was astonishing in his state. The girl kept staring wildly at his bloodstained hands, yet she too answered every question with wonderful readiness and speed, as if she were eager to give him the whole truth and nothing but the truth. Little by little, even with a kind of enjoyment, she began to explain every detail. She had no wish to torment him. She seemed eager to be as useful to him as she possibly could. She told him about the whole of that day, down to the smallest thing: the visit from Rakitin and Alyosha, how she, Fenya, had kept watch, how her mistress had set off, and how she had called out of the window to Alyosha, asking him to give Mitya her greetings and tell him “to remember for ever how she had loved him for an hour.”
At the news of this message, Mitya suddenly smiled, and color rose in his pale cheeks. Just then Fenya said to him, not the least bit afraid now of being nosy:
“Look at your hands, Dmitri Fyodorovitch. They’re all over blood!”
“Yes,” Mitya answered mechanically. He gave his hands a careless glance and at once forgot both them and Fenya’s question.

He fell silent again. Twenty minutes had gone by since he ran in. The first shock had passed, but it was plain that some new, fixed resolve had taken hold of him. He suddenly stood up, smiling dreamily.
“What’s happened to you, sir?” said Fenya, pointing at his hands again. She spoke with pity, as though she now felt very close to him in his grief. Mitya looked at his hands once more.

“That’s blood, Fenya,” he said, looking at her oddly. “That’s human blood, and, good God, why was it shed? But ... Fenya ... there’s a fence here” (he looked at her as if he were setting her a riddle), “a high fence, terrible to look at. But tomorrow at dawn, when the sun comes up, Mitya will jump over that fence.... You don’t understand what fence, Fenya, and never mind.... You’ll hear tomorrow and then you’ll understand ... and now, goodbye. I won’t stand in her way. I’ll step aside, I know how to step aside. Live, my joy.... You loved me for an hour, so remember Mityenka Karamazov for ever.... She always called me Mityenka, do you remember?”
And with those words he abruptly left the kitchen. This sudden exit frightened Fenya almost more than his rushing in and attacking her had.

Exactly ten minutes later Dmitri arrived at the house of Pyotr Ilyitch Perhotin, the young official he had pawned his pistols to. It was already half-past eight. Pyotr Ilyitch had finished his evening tea and had just put his coat back on, meaning to go to the “Metropolis” for a game of billiards. Mitya caught him on his way out.
At the sight of his face smeared with blood, the young man cried out in astonishment.
“Good heavens! What on earth has happened?”
“I’ve come for my pistols,” said Mitya, “and I’ve brought the money. Thanks very much. I’m in a hurry, Pyotr Ilyitch, so be quick, please.”

Pyotr Ilyitch was growing more and more astonished. He suddenly noticed a wad of banknotes in Mitya’s hand. Besides, Mitya had come in holding the notes in a way no one ever holds money: in his right hand, stretched out in front of him, as though to display them. Perhotin’s servant boy met Mitya in the passage, and said afterwards that he had walked into the passage in the same way, with the money stretched out in his hand, so he must have carried it like that even in the street. They were all hundred-rouble notes of the rainbow-colored kind, and the fingers that held them were covered with blood.

Later, when Pyotr Ilyitch was asked how much money it was, he said it was hard to tell at a glance, but it might have been two thousand, or maybe three. It was a big, “fat” bundle. “Dmitri Fyodorovitch,” he testified afterwards, “didn’t seem himself either. He wasn’t drunk, but he seemed, as it were, carried away, lost to everything around him, and at the same time absorbed, as though he were turning something over and searching for something and couldn’t decide. He was in a great hurry, he answered abruptly and very oddly, and at moments he seemed not at all gloomy but quite cheerful.”
“But what _is_ the matter with you? What’s wrong?” cried Pyotr Ilyitch, staring wildly at his visitor. “How did you get covered in blood? Did you fall? Look at yourself!”
He took him by the elbow and led him over to the mirror.
At the sight of his bloodstained face, Mitya gave a start and scowled furiously.

“Damn it! That’s the last straw,” he muttered angrily. He quickly shifted the notes from his right hand to his left and jerked the handkerchief out of his pocket on impulse. But the handkerchief turned out to be soaked with blood too (it was the one he had used to wipe Grigory’s face). There was hardly a white spot left on it. It hadn’t just begun to dry, either, but had stiffened into a crumpled ball that couldn’t be pulled apart. Mitya flung it angrily on the floor.
“Oh, damn it!” he said. “Haven’t you got some kind of rag ... to wipe my face?”
“So you’re just stained, not wounded? Then you’d better wash,” said Pyotr Ilyitch. “There’s the washstand. I’ll pour you some water.”
“A washstand? Fine ... but what am I to do with this?”
In the strangest bewilderment he pointed to his wad of hundred-rouble notes, looking at Pyotr Ilyitch as though it were for him to decide what Mitya should do with his own money.
“Put it in your pocket, or on the table here. It won’t go missing.”

“In my pocket? Yes, in my pocket. All right.... But, I say, all this is nonsense,” he cried, as if suddenly waking from his trance. “Look, let’s deal with the business of the pistols first. Give them back to me. Here’s your money ... because I need them badly ... and I haven’t a minute, not one minute to spare.”
And taking the top note off the wad, he held it out to Pyotr Ilyitch.
“But I won’t have enough change for that. Haven’t you got a smaller one?”
“No,” said Mitya, looking at the wad again, and as if he didn’t trust his own words, he flipped over two or three of the top notes.
“No, they’re all the same,” he added, and again looked at Pyotr Ilyitch as if asking him.
“How did you get so rich?” the other asked. “Wait, I’ll send my boy to Plotnikov’s. They stay open late. He’ll see if they can change it. Here, Misha!” he called into the passage.

“To Plotnikov’s shop, splendid!” cried Mitya, as though an idea had struck him. “Misha,” he said to the boy as he came in, “listen, run over to Plotnikov’s and tell them Dmitri Fyodorovitch sends his greetings and will be there in a moment.... But listen, listen, tell them to have champagne ready before I come, three dozen bottles, packed the way it was when it went to Mokroe. I took four dozen with me that time,” he added (suddenly addressing Pyotr Ilyitch). “They know all about it, don’t you worry, Misha,” he said, turning to the boy again. “Wait, listen. Tell them to put in cheese, Strasburg pies, smoked fish, ham, caviare, and everything, everything they have, up to a hundred roubles, or a hundred and twenty like last time.... But wait, don’t let them forget dessert: sweets, pears, watermelons, two or three or four—no, one melon will do—and chocolate, candy, toffee, fondants. In fact, everything I took to Mokroe before, three hundred roubles’ worth with the champagne ... let it be exactly the same again. And remember, Misha, if that is your name—His name is Misha, isn’t it?” He turned to Pyotr Ilyitch again.
“Hold on a minute,” Pyotr Ilyitch cut in, listening and watching him uneasily. “You’d better go and tell them yourself. He’ll get it wrong.”

“He will, I can see he will! Eh, Misha! Why, I was ready to kiss you for running this errand.... If you don’t get it wrong, there are ten roubles for you. Run along, hurry up.... Champagne’s the main thing, make them bring plenty of champagne. And brandy too, and red and white wine, and everything I had then.... They know what I had then.”

“But listen!” Pyotr Ilyitch interrupted, a little impatiently. “Let him just run and get the money changed and tell them not to close, and you go and give the order yourself.... Give him your note. Off you go, Misha! Look lively!”

Pyotr Ilyitch seemed to be hurrying Misha out on purpose. The boy was standing there with his mouth and eyes wide open, plainly understanding very little of Mitya’s orders, and gazing in amazement and terror at his bloodstained face and at the shaking, bloodstained fingers that held the notes.
“Now come and wash,” said Pyotr Ilyitch sternly. “Put the money on the table, or else in your pocket.... That’s it, come along. But take off your coat.”
And as he started helping him out of his coat, he cried out again:
“Look, your coat’s covered in blood too!”

“That ... that’s not the coat. Just a little on the sleeve here.... And that’s only here, where the handkerchief was. It must have soaked through. I must have sat on the handkerchief at Fenya’s, and the blood came through,” Mitya explained at once, with an astounding, childlike lack of awareness. Pyotr Ilyitch listened with a frown.
“Well, you must have been up to something. You must have been fighting with somebody,” he muttered.

They began to wash. Pyotr Ilyitch held the jug and poured the water. Mitya, in desperate haste, hardly soaped his hands (they were shaking, and Pyotr Ilyitch remembered that afterwards). But the young official insisted that he soap them properly and scrub them harder. As time went on he seemed to gain more and more authority over Mitya. It may be mentioned in passing that he was a young man of firm character.

“Look, your nails aren’t clean. Now rub your face, here, on your temples, by your ear.... Are you going out in that shirt? Where are you going? Look, the whole cuff of your right sleeve is covered in blood.”
“Yes, it’s all bloody,” Mitya remarked, looking at his shirt cuff.
“Then change your shirt.”

“I haven’t time. You see, I’ll ...” Mitya went on with the same trusting simplicity, drying his face and hands on the towel and putting on his coat. “I’ll turn it up at the wrist. It won’t show under the coat.... See?”

“Now tell me, what have you been up to? Fighting with somebody? In the tavern again, like last time? Have you been beating that captain again?” Pyotr Ilyitch asked him reproachfully. “Who have you been beating this time ... or killing, perhaps?”
“Nonsense!” said Mitya.
“What do you mean, ‘nonsense’?”
“Don’t worry,” said Mitya, and suddenly laughed. “I just smashed an old woman in the market-place.”
“Smashed? An old woman?”
“An old man!” cried Mitya, looking Pyotr Ilyitch straight in the face, laughing and shouting at him as if he were deaf.
“Confound it! An old woman, an old man.... Have you killed somebody?”

“We made it up. We had a row, and we made it up. At a place I know. We parted friends. A fool.... He’s forgiven me.... He must have forgiven me by now ... if he’d got up, he wouldn’t have forgiven me”—Mitya suddenly winked—“only damn him, you know, I say, Pyotr Ilyitch, damn him! Don’t worry about him! I don’t want to, right now!” Mitya snapped, firmly.

“Why on earth do you have to go picking fights with everybody? ... Like you did with that captain, over some trifle.... You’ve been brawling, and now you’re off on a spree. That’s you all over! Three dozen bottles of champagne, what do you want with all that?”

“Bravo! Now give me the pistols. Honestly, I haven’t a moment now. I’d love to have a talk with you, my dear fellow, but I’ve no time. And there’s no need, it’s too late for talking. Where’s my money? Where did I put it?” he cried, thrusting his hands into his pockets.

“You put it on the table ... yourself.... Here it is. Forgot already? Money’s like dirt or water to you, it seems. Here are your pistols. Strange, isn’t it? At six o’clock you pawned them for ten roubles, and now you’ve got thousands. Two or three, I’d say.”
“Three, you bet,” laughed Mitya, stuffing the notes into the side pocket of his trousers.
“You’ll lose it like that. Have you struck a gold mine?”

“Mines? Gold mines?” Mitya shouted at the top of his voice and burst into a roar of laughter. “Would you like to go to the mines, Perhotin? There’s a lady here who’ll hand over three thousand for you if you’ll only go. She did it for me, she’s so terribly fond of gold mines. Do you know Madame Hohlakov?”
“I don’t know her, but I’ve heard of her and I’ve seen her. Did she really give you three thousand? Really?” said Pyotr Ilyitch, eyeing him doubtfully.

“As soon as the sun rises tomorrow, as soon as Phœbus, ever young, flies upward, praising and glorifying God, you go to her, this Madame Hohlakov, and ask her whether she handed over that three thousand or not. Try and find out.”

“I don’t know what footing you’re on with her ... but since you say it so positively, I suppose she did give it to you. You’ve got the money in your hand, and instead of going to Siberia you’re spending it all.... Where are you really off to now, eh?”
“To Mokroe.”
“To Mokroe? But it’s night!”
“Once the lad had all, now the lad has naught,” Mitya cried suddenly.
“How, ‘naught’? You say that with all those thousands!”
“I’m not talking about thousands. Damn thousands! I’m talking about the female character.
Fickle is the heart of woman, Treacherous and full of vice;
I agree with Ulysses. That’s what he says.”
“I don’t understand you!”
“Am I drunk?”
“Not drunk, but worse.”
“I’m drunk in spirit, Pyotr Ilyitch, drunk in spirit! But that’s enough!”
“What are you doing, loading the pistol?”
“I’m loading the pistol.”

Mitya unfastened the pistol case, actually opened the powder horn, and carefully poured in the powder and rammed down the charge. Then he took the bullet and, before putting it in, held it up between two fingers in front of the candle.
“Why are you staring at the bullet?” asked Pyotr Ilyitch, watching him with uneasy curiosity.
“Oh, just a whim. Tell me, if you meant to put that bullet in your brain, would you look at it first or not?”
“Why look at it?”

“It’s going into my brain, so it’s interesting to look and see what it’s like. But that’s foolishness, a moment’s foolishness. There, that’s done,” he added, putting in the bullet and driving it home with the ramrod. “Pyotr Ilyitch, my dear fellow, that’s nonsense, all nonsense, and if only you knew what nonsense! Now give me a little piece of paper.”
“Here’s some paper.”
“No, a clean new sheet, writing paper. That’s right.”

And taking a pen from the table, Mitya swiftly wrote two lines, folded the paper in four and pushed it into his waistcoat pocket. He put the pistols in their case, locked it and kept it in his hand. Then he looked at Pyotr Ilyitch with a slow, thoughtful smile.
“Now, let’s go.”
“Where are we going? No, wait a minute.... Are you thinking of putting that bullet in your brain, perhaps?” Pyotr Ilyitch asked uneasily.
“I was fooling about the bullet! I want to live. I love life! You can be sure of that. I love golden-haired Phœbus and his warm light.... Dear Pyotr Ilyitch, do you know how to step aside?”
“What do you mean, ‘stepping aside’?”

“Making way. Making way for someone dear, and for someone I hate. And letting the one I hate become dear to me. That’s what making way means! And saying to them: God bless you, go your way, move on, while I—”
“While you—?”
“Enough, let’s go.”
“On my word, I’ll tell someone to stop you from going there,” said Pyotr Ilyitch, looking at him. “What are you going to Mokroe for, anyway?”
“There’s a woman there, a woman. That’s all you need to know. Shut up.”
“Listen, you’re a savage, but I’ve always liked you.... I’m worried.”
“Thanks, old fellow. A savage, you say. Savages, savages! That’s just what I keep saying. Savages! Why, here’s Misha! I’d forgotten him.”

Misha came running in, in a great hurry, with a handful of notes in change. He reported that everyone at the Plotnikovs’ was in a bustle. “They’re carrying out the bottles, and the fish, and the tea. It’ll all be ready in a minute.” Mitya grabbed ten roubles and handed them to Pyotr Ilyitch, then tossed another ten-rouble note to Misha.

“Don’t you dare do that!” cried Pyotr Ilyitch. “I won’t have it in my house. It’s a bad habit, it spoils people. Put your money away. Here, put it here. Why waste it? You’ll be glad of it tomorrow, and I’d bet you’ll be coming to borrow ten roubles from me again. Why do you keep stuffing the notes in your side pocket? Ah, you’ll lose them!”
“Listen, my dear fellow, let’s go to Mokroe together.”
“What would I go for?”
“Listen, let’s open a bottle right now and drink to life! I want a drink, and I especially want to drink with you. I’ve never drunk with you, have I?”
“All right, we can go to the ‘Metropolis.’ I was just on my way there.”
“No time for that. Let’s drink at the Plotnikovs’, in the back room. Want me to ask you a riddle?”
“Go ahead.”
Mitya took the piece of paper out of his waistcoat pocket, unfolded it and showed it. In a large, clear hand it said: “I punish myself for my whole life, my whole life I punish!”
“I’m definitely going to tell someone, I’ll go right now,” said Pyotr Ilyitch, after reading the paper.
“You won’t have time, my dear boy. Come and have a drink. March!”

Plotnikov’s shop was at the corner of the street, two doors down from Pyotr Ilyitch’s. It was the largest grocery shop in our town, and by no means a bad one. It belonged to some rich merchants. They kept everything you could get in a Petersburg shop: groceries of every sort, wines “bottled by the brothers Eliseyev,” fruit, cigars, tea, coffee, sugar, and so on. They always employed three shop assistants and two errand boys. Our part of the country had grown poorer, the landowners had gone away and trade had got worse. Even so, the grocery stores flourished as before, more prosperous every year, because there were plenty of buyers for their goods.

They were waiting for Mitya impatiently in the shop. They remembered vividly how, three or four weeks ago, he had bought wine and goods of every kind to the value of several hundred roubles, paid for in cash. (They would never have let him have anything on credit, of course.) They remembered that then, as now, he had held a bundle of hundred-rouble notes in his hand and scattered them at random. He hadn’t bargained or stopped to think, or cared to think, what use so much wine and food would be to him. The story went all over the town that, when he drove off to Mokroe with Grushenka that time, he had “spent three thousand in one night and the following day, and come back from the spree without a penny.” He had picked up a whole troop of gypsies (camped in our neighborhood at the time), who for two days took money off him without limit while he was drunk, and drank expensive wine without limit. People used to tell, laughing at Mitya, how he had given champagne to peasants with grimy hands, and treated the village women and girls to sweets and Strasburg pies. It was rather risky to laugh at Mitya to his face, but there was a lot of laughter behind his back, especially in the tavern. They laughed at his own artless, public admission that all he had got out of Grushenka by this “escapade” was “permission to kiss her foot, and that was the most she had allowed him.”

By the time Mitya and Pyotr Ilyitch reached the shop, they found a cart with three horses harnessed abreast, with bells, and Andrey the driver waiting for Mitya at the entrance. Inside the shop they had almost finished packing one box of provisions. They were only waiting for Mitya to arrive so they could nail it shut and put it in the cart. Pyotr Ilyitch was astounded.
“Where did this cart come from so quickly?” he asked Mitya.

“I met Andrey as I ran to your place, and told him to drive straight here to the shop. There’s no time to lose. Last time I went with Timofey, but now Timofey has gone on ahead of me with the witch. Will we be very late, Andrey?”

“They’ll only get there an hour before us, at most, maybe not even that. I got Timofey ready to start. I know how he’ll go. Their pace won’t be ours, Dmitri Fyodorovitch. How could it be? They won’t get there an hour earlier!” Andrey replied warmly. He was a lanky, red-haired driver of middle age, wearing a full-skirted coat, with a kaftan over his arm.
“Fifty roubles for vodka if we’re only an hour behind them.”
“I guarantee the time, Dmitri Fyodorovitch. Ech, they won’t be half an hour ahead of us, let alone an hour.”

Mitya bustled about seeing to things, but he gave his orders oddly, in a scattered, jumbled way. He would begin a sentence and forget the end of it. Pyotr Ilyitch found himself having to step in and help.
“Four hundred roubles’ worth, not less than four hundred roubles’ worth, just like last time,” Mitya ordered. “Four dozen champagne, not a bottle less.”
“What do you want with so much? What’s it for? Wait!” cried Pyotr Ilyitch. “What’s this box? What’s in it? Surely there isn’t four hundred roubles’ worth here?”

The eager shopmen began explaining, with oily politeness, that the first box held only half a dozen bottles of champagne and only “the most essential articles,” such as savories, sweets, toffee and so on. But the main part of the goods ordered would be packed and sent off, as on the previous occasion, in a special cart, also with three horses, traveling at full speed. It would arrive no more than an hour after Dmitri Fyodorovitch himself.
“No more than an hour! No more than an hour! And put in more toffee and fondants. The girls there are so fond of them,” Mitya insisted hotly.

“The fondants are all right. But what do you want with four dozen champagne? One would be enough,” said Pyotr Ilyitch, almost angry. He began haggling and asking for an itemized bill, and wouldn’t be satisfied. But he only managed to save a hundred roubles. In the end it was agreed that only three hundred roubles’ worth should be sent.
“Oh, go to the devil!” cried Pyotr Ilyitch, thinking better of it. “What’s it to me? Throw your money away, since it cost you nothing.”

“This way, my economist, this way, don’t be angry.” Mitya drew him into a room at the back of the shop. “They’ll bring us a bottle here in a minute. We’ll taste it. Ech, Pyotr Ilyitch, come along with me, you’re a nice fellow, the sort I like.”

Mitya sat down on a wicker chair in front of a little table covered with a dirty napkin. Pyotr Ilyitch sat down opposite. The champagne soon appeared, and oysters were suggested to the gentlemen. “First-class oysters, the last lot in.”
“Oh, hang the oysters. I don’t eat them. And we don’t need a thing,” cried Pyotr Ilyitch, almost angrily.
“There’s no time for oysters,” said Mitya. “And I’m not hungry. Do you know, friend,” he said suddenly, with feeling, “I’ve never liked all this disorder.”
“Who does like it? Three dozen champagne for peasants, On my word, that’s enough to make anyone angry!”

“That’s not what I mean. I’m talking about a higher order. There’s no order in me, no higher order. But ... that’s all over. There’s no need to grieve about it. It’s too late, damn it! My whole life has been disorder, and now it has to be set in order. Is that a pun, eh?”
“You’re raving, not punning!”
“Glory be to God in Heaven, Glory be to God in me....
“That verse came from my heart once. It’s not a verse, it’s a tear.... I made it myself ... though not while I was pulling the captain’s beard....”
“Why do you bring him up all of a sudden?”
“Why do I bring him up? Foolery! Everything comes to an end; everything is made equal. That’s the long and short of it.”
“You know, I keep thinking about your pistols.”

“That’s all foolery too! Drink, and don’t get fanciful. I love life. I’ve loved life too much, shamefully much. Enough! Let’s drink to life, dear boy, I propose the toast. Why am I pleased with myself? I’m a scoundrel, but I’m satisfied with myself. And yet I’m tortured by the thought that I’m a scoundrel and satisfied with myself. I bless creation. I’m ready to bless God and His creation this minute, but ... I must kill one noxious insect, for fear it crawls about and spoils life for others.... Let us drink to life, dear brother. What can be more precious than life? Nothing! To life, and to one queen of queens!”
“Let’s drink to life, and to your queen too, if you like.”
They drank a glass each. Mitya was excited and expansive, but he was melancholy too. It was as if some heavy, crushing anxiety were weighing on him.
“Misha ... here’s your Misha come! Misha, come here, my boy, drink this glass to Phœbus, the golden-haired, of tomorrow morning....”
“What are you giving it to him for?” cried Pyotr Ilyitch irritably.
“Yes, yes, yes, let me! I want to!”
“E—ech!”
Misha emptied the glass, bowed, and ran out.

“He’ll remember that later,” Mitya remarked. “Woman, I love woman! And what is woman? The queen of creation! My heart is sad, my heart is sad, Pyotr Ilyitch. Do you remember Hamlet? ‘I am very sorry, good Horatio! Alas, poor Yorick!’ Maybe that’s me, Yorick? Yes, I’m Yorick now, and a skull later.”
Pyotr Ilyitch listened in silence. Mitya was silent for a while too.
“What dog is that you’ve got here?” he asked the shopman casually. He had noticed a pretty little lap dog with dark eyes sitting in the corner.
“It belongs to Varvara Alexyevna, the mistress,” answered the clerk. “She brought it and forgot it here. It has to be taken back to her.”

“I saw one like it ... in the regiment ...” murmured Mitya dreamily, “only that one had a broken hind leg.... By the way, Pyotr Ilyitch, I wanted to ask you: have you ever stolen anything in your life?”
“What a question!”
“Oh, I didn’t mean anything. From someone’s pocket, you know. I don’t mean government money, everyone steals that, and no doubt you do too....”
“Go to the devil.”
“I’m talking about other people’s money. Stealing straight out of a pocket? Out of a purse, eh?”
“I stole twenty kopecks from my mother when I was nine years old. I took it off the table on the sly, and held it tight in my hand.”
“Well, and what happened?”
“Nothing much. I kept it for three days, then I was ashamed, owned up, and gave it back.”
“And then?”
“Naturally I was whipped. But why do you ask? Have you stolen something?”
“I have,” said Mitya, winking slyly.
“What did you steal?” asked Pyotr Ilyitch, curious.
“I stole twenty kopecks from my mother when I was nine years old, and gave it back three days later.”
As he said this, Mitya suddenly got up.
“Dmitri Fyodorovitch, are you coming now?” called Andrey from the door of the shop.

“Are you ready? We’re coming!” Mitya started. “A few last words and—Andrey, a glass of vodka for the start. Give him some brandy as well! That box” (the one with the pistols) “put under my seat. Good-by, Pyotr Ilyitch, don’t hold anything against me.”
“But you’re coming back tomorrow?”
“Of course.”
“Will you settle the little bill now?” cried the clerk, springing forward.
“Oh, yes, the bill. Of course.”

He pulled the bundle of notes out of his pocket again, picked out three hundred roubles, threw them on the counter, and hurried out of the shop. Everyone followed him out, bowing and wishing him good luck. Andrey jumped up on the box, coughing from the brandy he had just swallowed. But Mitya was only just taking his seat when, to his surprise, he saw Fenya in front of him. She ran up panting, clasped her hands before him with a cry, and dropped down at his feet.

“Dmitri Fyodorovitch, dear good Dmitri Fyodorovitch, don’t hurt my mistress. And it was me who told you everything.... And don’t murder him, he was there first, he’s hers! He’s going to marry Agrafena Alexandrovna now. That’s why he’s come back from Siberia. Dmitri Fyodorovitch, dear, don’t take another human being’s life!”

“Tut—tut—tut! That’s it, is it? So you’re off there to make trouble!” muttered Pyotr Ilyitch. “Now it’s all clear, clear as daylight. Dmitri Fyodorovitch, give me your pistols right now, if you mean to behave like a man,” he shouted to Mitya. “Do you hear, Dmitri?”

“The pistols? Wait a bit, brother, I’ll throw them into the pool on the road,” answered Mitya. “Fenya, get up, don’t kneel to me. Mitya won’t hurt anyone, the silly fool won’t ever hurt anyone again. But listen, Fenya,” he shouted, after taking his seat. “I hurt you just now, so forgive me and have pity on me, forgive a scoundrel.... But it doesn’t matter if you don’t. It’s all the same now. Now then, Andrey, look alive, fly along at full speed!”
Andrey whipped up the horses, and the bells began ringing.
“Good-by, Pyotr Ilyitch! My last tear is for you!...”

“He’s not drunk, but he keeps babbling like a lunatic,” Pyotr Ilyitch thought as he watched him go. He had half a mind to stay and watch the cart being packed with the remaining wines and provisions. He knew they would cheat and defraud Mitya. But suddenly he felt annoyed with himself, turned away with a curse and went to the tavern to play billiards.

“He’s a fool, but he’s a good fellow,” he muttered as he went. “I’ve heard about that officer, Grushenka’s old flame. Well, if he has turned up.... Ech, those pistols! Damn it all! I’m not his nurse! Let them do as they please! Besides, it’ll all come to nothing. They’re brawlers, that’s all. They’ll drink and fight, fight and make up again. They’re not men who do anything real. What does he mean by ‘I’m stepping aside, I’m punishing myself’? It’ll come to nothing! He’s shouted phrases like that a thousand times, drunk, in the taverns. But now he’s not drunk. ‘Drunk in spirit’—they’re fond of fine phrases, the villains. Am I his nurse? He must have been fighting, his face was covered in blood. Who with? I’ll find out at the ‘Metropolis.’ And his handkerchief was soaked in blood.... It’s still lying on my floor.... Hang it!”

He reached the tavern in a bad mood and at once got up a game. The game cheered him. He played a second game, and suddenly began telling one of his partners that Dmitri Karamazov had come into cash again, something like three thousand roubles, and had gone to Mokroe again to spend it with Grushenka.... This news roused strange interest in his listeners. They all talked about it, not laughing, but with odd seriousness. They stopped playing.
“Three thousand? But where could he have got three thousand?”
Questions were asked. The story of Madame Hohlakov’s gift was received with skepticism.
“Hasn’t he robbed his old father?—that’s the question.”
“Three thousand! There’s something odd about it.”
“He boasted aloud that he would kill his father. We all heard him, right here. And it was three thousand he talked about ...”
Pyotr Ilyitch listened. All at once his answers became short and dry. He said not a word about the blood on Mitya’s face and hands, though he had meant to mention it at first.

They began a third game, and little by little the talk about Mitya died away. But by the end of the third game Pyotr Ilyitch had no more desire for billiards. He laid down the cue and, without having supper as he had intended, walked out of the tavern. When he reached the market place he stood still in bewilderment, wondering at himself. He realized that what he wanted was to go to Fyodor Pavlovitch’s and find out whether anything had happened there. “Over some stupid nonsense—as it’s sure to turn out—am I going to wake up the household and make a scandal? Fooh! Damn it, is it my business to look after them?”

In a very bad mood he went straight home, and suddenly remembered Fenya. “Damn it all! I should have questioned her just now,” he thought with annoyance. “I’d have heard everything.” And the wish to speak to her and find out became so pressing and insistent that, halfway home, he turned sharply and went toward the house where Grushenka lodged. Going up to the gate he knocked. The sound of the knock in the silence of the night sobered him and made him feel irritated. And no one answered him; everyone in the house was asleep.
“And I’ll be making a fuss!” he thought, feeling thoroughly uncomfortable. But instead of going away altogether, he started knocking again with all his might, filling the street with noise.
“Not coming? Well, I’ll wake them up, I will!” he muttered at each knock, fuming at himself. But at the same time he knocked even harder on the gate.
